newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia says Cambodian "civil war" dooms peace.
newsitem.headline: Australia says Cambodian "civil war" dooms peace.

text.p: Australia said on Monday Cambodia was now embroiled in civil war and that the country's 1991 peace accords appeared doomed.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard said two military aircraft had been sent to Malaysia and were on stand-by to evacuate 517 Australians and 150 Canadians.

The international airport in the capital Phnom Penh has been closed since Saturday when fighting erupted. At least 12 people were killed and more than 50 wounded in a weekend of fighting on the streets of the capital.
"It is a very difficult, unstable situation when you have outbreaks of violence and essentially civil war of this kind, foreigners can get caught in the crossfire," Howard told reporters.

"At this stage they (Australians and Canadians) are in no more or less danger than any other foreigners in a very difficult situation. The latest advice I had a few hours ago was that none of them had been injured," he said.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said Cambodia's warring coalition government had collapsed and the October 1991 Paris peace accords ending three decades of fighting were unravelling.
"Clearly, the breakdown in the coalition is now irretrievable," Downer said in a radio interview.

"It's a tragic thing that the coalition that we hoped would remain in place until May of next year, when elections are scheduled to be held, has fallen apart in this sort of way. I do think the Paris peace accords are starting to unravel."
Downer said fighting between troops loyal to royalist First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, a former communist ruler, had died down considerably overnight.

But it appeared Hun Sen's Cambodian People's Party (CPP) had taken control of the capital, Downer said. "It would appear that the CPP forces have taken...90 percent of Phnom Penh and presumably seized control of the levers of government."

Hun Sen and Ranariddh formed an uneasy coalition government after United Nations-run elections in 1993, held under the 1991 peace accord. But the alliance has never been close and tensions and political violence have worsened over recent months.
A leading Cambodian expert, David Chandler, author of the Pol Pot biography "Brother Number One", said the outbreak of violence was aimed at ensuring a Hun Sen victory at next year's election.

"I think it indicates an attempt by Hun Sen and his group to pre-emptively cut off and reduce the power of the other political party in the run up for elections," said Chandler, head of the Centre of Southeast Asian Studies at Monash University in Melbourne.
"I think Hun Sen really wants to arrive at those elections without much opposition," Chandler said.
Australia said the international community should push for next year's elections to go ahead as scheduled.
"There's no reason at this stage to believe the elections won't take place, but...it's important the elections are free, fair and open," Downer said.
